summary: Eastern entrance to the Santa Barbara Channel: an 1874 wooden keeper's-house light, moved in 1940 and demolished; the 1941 concrete tower is automated.

structures.type: square, Art Moderne, on fog signal building

access.note: On Coast Guard ground at the end of the public beach promenade. A 2010 article says it has been open to tours on certain days; the archive record says it is not open to the public.

events.note: Samuel Ensign took charge as principal keeper, 9 November 1874
Board recommended $7,000 for a steam fog signal (1882). Museum: approved and installed; LighthouseFriends: never provided; Ward: station later outfitted with a fog signal (no date)
Flashing white changed to fixed red, 1 April 1889
Fixed red changed to occulting white (Ward: 15 April 1892)
Fresnel lens installed (Museum and county); Ward also dates a Fresnel lens to 1897
Board records a change of characteristic on 10 January 1899; LighthouseFriends dates a new revolving fourth-order Fresnel lens to 1899
First-class siren fog signal established; Museum gives $18,000 for pneumatic equipment
Old light moved across the harbor entrance, February 1940
Concrete Art Moderne tower (48 ft) dedicated; original Fresnel lens reused
Light blacked out the evening after the declaration of war
Ventura County Landmark No. 57 (text gives 1 October 1979; footer gives 1980)

corrections.why: The 1874 tower was wood, on the keeper's dwelling; the concrete Art Moderne tower was dedicated in 1941 (county; roster gives 48 ft).

corrections.proposed: remove, unless a primary source shows a 1975 deactivation
corrections.why: The light was automated in 1972 and the roster shows keepers to 1968; the county record describes the light as operating. No source I read gives 1975.

corrections.proposed: verify against the current Light List before use
corrections.why: The county says the lightworks throws a beam every five seconds, and no source read gives a red light. Not applied.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1874 is the first tower (wood, on the keeper's house); 1941 is the present concrete tower, dedicated after the 1940 move. The record's two first years belong to two different buildings.

The characteristics the record lists belong to different years: flashing white to 1889, fixed red 1889-1892, occulting white 1892-1899; the Board's 1899 report says the occulting apparatus was taken out and a lens with flashing white characteristics substituted, which LighthouseFriends calls a revolving fourth-order Fresnel lens with a white flash every five seconds.

The Board recommended $7,000 in 1882. The Museum says Congress approved it quickly and a signal followed; LighthouseFriends says the money was never provided; Ward says the station was later outfitted with a fog signal, with no date. The story states all three; no primary record read settles it.
Ward quotes the 1882 report: the artesian water was unfit for domestic use and caused sickness, and a tank was put up. The Museum says saltwater had invaded the well. The story gives both.

resolved_conflicts.field: right of way and condemnation date
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1893 report says the efforts had failed and that it was decided to obtain title by condemnation; the record's 'by 1894' is the 1894 report repeating the plan. The earlier story footnote named the wrong report year (1894 for a page of the 1893 report); corrected.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on dates, and the story states the disagreements. (1) Lens: Ward describes a fourth-order Fresnel lens at first lighting and a second Fresnel lens in 1897; the Museum and county date the Fresnel lens to 1897; the 1899 Board entry is a change of characteristic. (2) New tower: county says dedicated 1941; Museum says the year after the 1940 move. (3) Demolition: Ward says after the 1942 Navy takeover; county says 1943. (4) Landmark: text 1 October 1979, footer 1980. (5) Reservation: county 60 acres; Museum and Ward 30 acres. (6) Allen: roster lists acting 1894 and principal 1911-1914; Museum gives 1894-1915. (7) Anna H. Allen is an acting principal in 1911 on the archive roster only; no other source names her. (8) Giles: Museum says promoted after being twice caught asleep; LighthouseFriends says principal keeper at Pigeon Point in August 1875; the roster lists only a first-assistant stint 1874-1875. (9) 1882 fog signal: Museum says approved and installed; LighthouseFriends says never provided; Ward says outfitted, no date. (10) 1882 well: Ward quotes unfit water and sickness; Museum says saltwater. (11) Ensign's 1878 dismissal: Museum says failure to keep the grounds; LighthouseFriends says physical incapacity. (12) Ward's 1930s photo caption names 'former keeper Richard White'; the roster and Museum name Walter White (1927-1948). Not used. (13) The 1901 report says a lens 'formerly in use at Point Hueneme' went to Point Arguello, which conflicts with the Museum's account that the 1897 lens was reused in 1941. Not used. (14) Wikipedia not used. The 1882 Board report was not in the local corpus; the story relies on Ward quoting it, and the 1912 Bulletin and corpus Board reports are cited directly. (15) Roster: all lines checked against the archive place page (archives.uslhs.org/places/point-hueneme); names are printed as the archive prints them, duplicates (John Ross 1880-1882) kept once. Thomas M. Ward (article author) is not George S. Ward (keeper, 1938-1957). (16) Current characteristic and range are unverified; the record's 5.0 nm range has no source read. (17) Visiting: the Museum says tours on some days and that visitors may climb to the lantern room on open days; the archive says not open to the public. The story says to check first and not to climb without arranged access. (18) Matched by position: none; no table column was read for a name in this story.
